entry.title: We Still Need Human Intelligence: The Part Beyond Measure

link.title: We Still Need Human Intelligence: The Part Beyond Measure

entry.content:
阅读中文版

Wit beyond measure is man’s greatest treasure. — J.K. Rowling

Agents, represented by large language models, have made unimaginable strides in recent years: they write prose swiftly and eloquently, derive mathematical proofs rapidly and accurately, and generate code that is both precise and concise. Before long, agents may truly integrate into our daily lives and take over a vast amount of our work. This inevitably raises profound questions: What will agents look like in five or ten years? Will our work still require human involvement? Where does the true boundary of an agent lie?

Borrowing the lens of reinforcement learning pioneer Rich Sutton in The Bitter Lesson, we can view today’s agents as a paradigm that successfully scales through Search and Learning:

  • Search here means: Given an input, the agent selects the next output token one by one from a space of candidate tokens until termination.
  • Learning here means: Through next-token prediction methods—whether via supervised learning, reinforcement learning, or diffusion—the agent learns how to search for the next token.
flowchart LR

    classDef candidate fill:#fafafa,stroke:#d9d9d9,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#595959;

    Root["I"]:::selected
    C1_am["am"]:::candidate
    C1_have["have"]:::selected
    C1_like["like"]:::candidate
    C2_happy["happy"]:::candidate
    C2_learning["learning"]:::candidate
    C2_a["a"]:::selected
    C2_been["been"]:::candidate
    C2_no["no"]:::candidate
    C2_to["to"]:::candidate
    C2_apples["apples"]:::candidate
    C3_dream["dream"]:::selected
    C3_chance["chance"]:::candidate
    C3_car["car"]:::candidate

    Root --> C1_am
    Root ==> C1_have
    Root --> C1_like
    C1_am --> C2_happy
    C1_am --> C2_learning
    C1_have ==> C2_a
    C1_have --> C2_been
    C1_have --> C2_no
    C1_like --> C2_to
    C1_like --> C2_apples
    C2_a ==> C3_dream
    C2_a --> C3_chance
    C2_a --> C3_car

    linkStyle 1,5,10 stroke:#ff4d4f,stroke-width:3.5px;

The mission of artificial intelligence is to study and understand “intelligence.” If we adopt Sutton’s definition—intelligence is the domain-independent part of the ability to achieve goals—then what we are currently confident in realizing is precisely the “search” component of it.

We can naturally generalize this notion of search: anything that follows the loop of “being in a current state $\rightarrow$ selecting an action $\rightarrow$ transitioning to the next state” can be handled by this search paradigm. Writing, for instance, is selecting the next word given a sequence of preceding words; sweeping the floor, likewise, is naturally deciding where to clean next given the current layout of clean and messy areas. This is the premise upon which future agents will achieve widespread adoption: search-based methods are sufficient to handle the vast majority of tasks in our daily lives and work. Moreover, agent-based search is vastly cheaper than human search. Herein lies the root of our anxiety—the fear that AI will replace most jobs, leaving us with nowhere to stand.

Yet I believe this anxiety magnifies what we need not fear, while overlooking what truly warrants our vigilance.

First, let us look at the magnified, unnecessary anxiety.

On the one hand, search-based intelligence is by no means the entirety of intelligence; on the other hand, the real world is far larger than any world an agent can model. Search-based agents can certainly solve complex mathematical problems, but many “flashes of insight” cannot be cheaply found through search. Within human intelligence, there remains much that is not search-based—elements that may not always drive earth-shattering paradigm shifts, yet tangibly help us do our everyday work better. As for what this “non-search intelligence” specifically entails, we may not yet have a complete definition, and figuring that out is a task left for all of us. What we truly ought to do is offload more of the “search” part of our intellect to external agents, leveraging their efficient search to explore the next frontier of human wisdom.

Second, let us examine where people may be overly optimistic.

Many fall into blind optimism because they mistake tasks where “I am still capable, and agents temporarily fall short” for the true boundaries of agents. Examples include processing multimodal inputs, executing physical actions in the real world, or capabilities people used to cherish—such as long-horizon planning, making final executive calls, or even bearing responsibility and accountability. In truth, under the logic of “search versus non-search,” none of these represent the true boundary of intelligence: the former still fall within the broad category of state-action search, while the latter are merely divisions of rules within human society. We should certainly acknowledge that there are things agents cannot do, but we need to rethink and anticipate what kind of world we will inhabit, and how we should adapt to it.

In short, today’s agents can be viewed as search-based systems capable of accomplishing feats that were once—and even now remain—hard to imagine. Yet at the same time, we still possess “wit beyond measure,” and that remains our greatest treasure. Perhaps in 10 or 20 years, search-based intelligence will genuinely enter the everyday scenarios I have predicted. And it is precisely as the boundary of search continues to expand that we will peel back the layers and see, with growing clarity, the parts of human intelligence that do not belong to search—thereby truly understanding ourselves and this brave new world.
entry.summary: Reflections on search-based agents and the part of human intelligence beyond measure.

entry.title: 我们依然需要人类的智慧，无法衡量的部分

link.title: 我们依然需要人类的智慧，无法衡量的部分

entry.content:
Read in English

无法衡量的智慧，是人最大的财富。 —— J.K. 罗琳

以大模型为代表的智能体（Agents）在过去一段时间里取得了超乎想象的进步：它们可以把文章写得又快又好，把数学推导得又快又对，把代码写得既准确又简洁。未来，智能体或许能够真正进入我们的日常生活，完成大量的工作。这不得不引人深思：五年后、十年后的智能体会是什么样？我们的工作是否还需要人的参与？智能体的边界究竟在哪里？

借用强化学习先驱 Rich Sutton 在 The Bitter Lesson 中的视角，我们可以将如今的智能体视为一种在搜索（Search）与学习（Learning）下成功扩展的范式：

  • 这里的搜索：给定一段输入，智能体在备选的 token 空间中，一个接一个地选择下一个输出的 token，直到结束。
  • 这里的学习：智能体通过预测下一个 token 的方法（无论是监督学习、强化学习还是 Diffusion），学习如何去搜索下一个 token。

    C2_to["to"]:::candidate

    Root --> C1_am
    Root ==> C1_have

    C2_a --> C3_chance
    C2_a --> C3_car

    linkStyle 1,5,10 stroke:#ff4d4f,stroke-width:3.5px;

人工智能的使命是研究并理解“智能”。如果借用 Sutton 的定义——智能是实现目标的能力中与具体领域无关的那部分（Intelligence is the domain-independent part of the ability to achieve goals）——那么目前我们有信心实现的，正是其中“搜索”的部分。

我们可以很自然地泛化这种搜索：任何“处于当前状态 $\rightarrow$ 选择动作 $\rightarrow$ 进入下一个状态”的事物，都可以被这种搜索范式所处理。例如文字类的工作，是在一系列当前文字下，选择接下来的文字；再如扫地，处于当前干净或脏乱的区域，我们会自然考虑下一步如何打扫。这是未来智能体能够得到广泛发展的前提：基于搜索的方法，足以处理日常生活和工作中的大部分任务。 并且，基于智能体的搜索比人类自己做搜索要便宜得多——这正是我们焦虑的根源：担心人工智能取代绝大部分岗位，而我们终将无所适从。

但我认为，这种焦虑放大了不必要担忧的部分，却忽略了真正值得警惕的部分。

首先来看被放大的、不必要的焦虑。

一方面，基于搜索的智能，绝不是智能的全部；另一方面，真实世界比任何一个智能体能够建模的世界都要大得多。基于搜索的智能体当然可以解决很多复杂的数学问题，但许多“灵光乍现”的点子，并不能靠基于搜索的方法很便宜地搜出来。在人类的智慧中，还有许多不基于搜索的部分——它们未必是惊天动地的范式转移，却实实在在地帮助我们把日常工作做得更好。至于这些“非搜索的智慧”具体是什么，我们现在或许还无法给出一个完备的定义，但这本来就是留给我们所有人的课题。我们真正应该做的，是把智力中属于“搜索”的部分更多地转移给外界的智能体，借助外物的高效搜索，并探索人类智慧的下一步。

其次来看目前大家可能过分乐观的部分。

很多人之所以盲目乐观，是因为把一些“目前我还行、智能体暂时做不到”的事情，误当成了智能体真正的边界。例如处理多模态的输入、在真实世界中执行物理动作；又或者以前人们常说的“执行长程规划的能力”、“拍板做决策的能力”，甚至是“承担责任的能力”。其实，从“搜索与非搜索”的逻辑来看，这些都算不上智能真正的边界——前几项依然属于广义的状态-动作搜索范畴，而后几项更多是人类社会的规则划分。我们当然应该承认智能体做不了某些事情，但我们需要重新认知和推测：我们将处于一个什么样的世界，又该如何去适应这个世界。

总之，目前的智能体可以视作是基于搜索的，它们能够完成许多过去乃至未来都难以想象的事情。但与此同时，我们依然拥有目前“无法衡量的智慧”，这正是我们最大的财富。 或许未来 10 年、20 年后，基于搜索的智能真的可以进入我所预测的这些日常场景；而恰恰是在搜索边界不断拓展的过程中，我们也能像剥茧抽丝一样，越来越清晰地看清人类智能中那些“不属于搜索”的部分，从而真正认识我们自己，认识这个新的世界。
entry.summary: 关于智能体的搜索能力与人类无法衡量的智慧的思考。

entry.title: Concentration Inequalities for Reinforcement Learning
entry.content:
This note collects concentration inequalities that frequently appear in reinforcement learning analysis. It is meant as a working reference rather than a complete survey.

1. Markov inequality and Chernoff bound

If \(X\) is a nonnegative random variable and \(a>0\), then the probability that \(X\) is at least \(a\) is at most the expectation of \(X\) divided by \(a\):

\[\mathrm{P}(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\mathrm{E}(X)}{a}\]

In probability theory, Markov’s inequality gives an upper bound on the probability that a non-negative random variable is greater than or equal to some positive constant. Markov’s inequality is tight in the sense that for each chosen positive constant, there exists a random variable such that the inequality is in fact an equality.

The generic Chernoff bound for a random variable \(X\) is attained by applying Markov’s inequality to \(e^{t X}\) (which is why it is sometimes called the exponential Markov or exponential moments bound). For positive \(t\) this gives a bound on the right tail of \(X\) in terms of its moment-generating function \(M(t)=\mathrm{E}\left(e^{t X}\right)\):

\[\mathrm{P}(X \geq a)=\mathrm{P}\left(e^{t X} \geq e^{t a}\right) \leq M(t) e^{-t a} \quad(t>0)\]

Chernoff bound is an exponentially decreasing upper bound on the tail of a random variable based on its moment generating function.

It is a sharper bound than the first- or second-moment-based tail bounds such as Markov’s inequality or Chebyshev’s inequality, which only yield power-law bounds on tail decay. However, when applied to sums the Chernoff bound requires the random variables to be independent, a condition that is not required by either Markov’s inequality or Chebyshev’s inequality.

The Chernoff bound is related to the Bernstein inequalities. It is also used to prove Hoeffding’s inequality, Bennett’s inequality, and McDiarmid’s inequality.

2. Hoeffding’s inequality

Suppose \(X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots, X_{n}\) are a sequence of independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with mean \(\mu\). Let \(\bar{X}_{n} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\). Suppose that \(X_{i} \in [b_{-}, b_{+}]\) with probability 1, then

\[P (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq \mu + \epsilon) \leq e ^ {- 2 n \epsilon^ {2} / (b _ {+} - b _ {-}) ^ {2}}.\]

Similarly,

\[P (\bar {X} _ {n} \leq \mu - \epsilon) \leq e ^ {- 2 n \epsilon^ {2} / (b _ {+} - b _ {-}) ^ {2}}.\]

The Chernoff bound implies that with probability \(1 - \delta\):

\[\bar {X} _ {n} - E X \leq (b _ {+} - b _ {-}) \sqrt {\ln (1 / \delta) / (2 n)}.\]

Hoeffding’s inequality is a special case of the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality and McDiarmid’s inequality. It is similar to the Chernoff bound, but tends to be less sharp, in particular when the variance of the random variables is small.

3. Sub-Gaussian Random Variable

A random variable \(X\) is \(\sigma\)-subGaussian if for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\), it holds that \(\mathbb{E}[\exp (\lambda X)] \leq \exp (\lambda^2\sigma^2 / 2)\).

One can show that a Gaussian random variable with zero mean and standard deviation \(\sigma\) is a \(\sigma\)-subGaussian random variable.

The following theorem shows that the tails of a \(\sigma\)-subGaussian random variable decay approximately as fast as that of a Gaussian variable with zero mean and standard deviation \(\sigma\).

The following lemma shows that the sum of independent sub-Gaussian variables is still sub-Gaussian.

Lemma 1. Suppose that \(X_{1}\) and \(X_{2}\) are independent and \(\sigma_{1}\) and \(\sigma_{2}\) subGaussian, respectively. Then for any \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), we have \(cX\) being \(\vert c \vert \sigma\)-subGaussian. We also have \(X_{1} + X_{2}\) being \(\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}\)-subGaussian.

4. Hoeffding-Azuma Inequality

Definition 1 (Martingale Difference Sequence, M. D. S.). A sequence of random variables \(\{X_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is called a martingale difference sequence, or m. d. s., with respect to a filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\) if for all \(n, \mathbb{E}[\vert X_{n}\vert]<\infty, X_{n} \in \mathcal{F}_{n}\), and \(\mathbb{E}[X_{n} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=0\) hold.

As the name implies, the sum sequence of a martingale difference sequence is called a martingale.

The Azuma-Hoeffding inequality provides an exponentially decaying tail bound for the sum of a martingale difference sequence:

Suppose \(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{N}\) is a martingale difference sequence where each \(X_{i}\) is a \(\sigma_i\) sub-Gaussian. Then, for all \(\epsilon >0\) and all positive integer \(K\):

\[P \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} X _ {i} \geq \epsilon\right) \leq \exp \left(\frac {- \epsilon^ {2}}{2 \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}\right).\]

5. Bernstein’s Inequality

Lemma 2 (Bernstein’s inequality). Suppose \(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{n}\) are independent random variables. Let \(\bar{X}_n = n^{-1}\sum_{i = 1}^n X_i\), \(\mu = \mathbb{E}\bar{X}_n\), and \(Var(X_{i})\) denote the variance of \(X_{i}\). If \(X_{i} - EX_{i}\leq b\) for all \(i\), then

\[P (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq \mu + \epsilon) \leq \exp \left[ - \frac {n ^ {2} \epsilon^ {2}}{2 \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \operatorname {V a r} (X _ {i}) + 2 n b \epsilon / 3} \right].\]

If all the variances are equal, the Bernstein inequality implies that, with probability at least \(1 - \delta\),

\[\bar {X} _ {n} - E X \leq \sqrt {2 \mathrm {V a r} (X) \ln (1 / \delta) / n} + \frac {2 b \ln (1 / \delta)}{3 n}.\]

Lemma 3 (Bernstein’s Inequality for Martingales). Suppose \(X_{1}, X_{2} \ldots\) is a martingale difference sequence where \(\vert X_{i}\vert \leq M \in \mathbb{R}^{+}\) almost surely. Then for all positive \(t\) and \(n \in \mathbb{N}^{+}\), we have:

\[P \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} \geq t\right) \leq \exp \left(- \frac {t ^ {2} / 2}{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbb {E} \left[ X _ {i} ^ {2} \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1} \right] + M t / 3}\right).\]

6. Concentration for Discrete Distributions

Let \(z\) be a discrete random variable that takes values in \(\{1,\dots ,d\}\), distributed according to \(q\). We write \(q\) as a vector where \(\vec{q} = [\mathrm{Pr}(z = j)]_{j = 1}^{d}\). Assume we have \(N\) i. i. d samples, and that our empirical estimate of \(\vec{q}\) is \([\hat{q}]_j = \sum_{i = 1}^N\mathbf{1}[z_i = j] / N\).

We have that \(\forall \epsilon > 0\):

\[\Pr \left(\| \widehat {q} - \bar {q} \| _ {2} \geq 1 / \sqrt {N} + \epsilon\right) \leq e ^ {- N \epsilon^ {2}}.\]

which implies that:

\[\operatorname * {P r} \left(\| \widehat {q} - \overline \| _ {1} \geq \sqrt {d} (1 / \sqrt {N} + \epsilon)\right) \leq e ^ {- N \epsilon^ {2}}.\]

This result illustrates that the \(L_2\) bound is tighter than the \(L_1\) bound by roughly \(\sqrt{d}\). Geometrically, this stems from the fact that the \(L_2\) norm is Euclidean distance (straight line), whereas the \(L_1\) norm is Manhattan distance (grid path). Thus the \(L_1\) bound incurs an additional \(\sqrt{d}\) factor in the worst case.

Intuitively, for any fixed vector, a higher-order norm yields a smaller value (i.e., tighter distance). We have the following relationship for \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\):

\[\|x\|_{\infty} \leq\|x\|_{2} \leq\|x\|_{1} \leq \sqrt{d}\|x\|_{2} \leq d\|x\|_{\infty}.\]

7. Self-Normalized Bound for Vector-Valued Martingales

Let \(\{\varepsilon_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}\) be a real-valued stochastic process with corresponding filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}\) such that \(\varepsilon_i\) is \(\mathcal{F}_i\) measurable, \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}] = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_i\) is conditionally \(\sigma\)-subGaussian with \(\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+\). Let \(\{X_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}\) be a stochastic process with \(X_i \in \mathcal{H}\) (some Hilbert space) and \(X_i\) being \(\mathcal{F}_t\) measurable. Assume that a linear operator \(\Sigma: \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{H}\) is positive definite, i.e., \(x^\top \Sigma x > 0\) for any \(x \in \mathcal{H}\). For any \(t\), define the linear operator \(\Sigma_t = \Sigma_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} X_i X_i^\top\) (here \(xx^\top\) denotes outer-product in \(\mathcal{H}\)). With probability at least \(1 - \delta\), we have for all \(t \geq 1\):

\[\left\| \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {t} X _ {i} \varepsilon_ {i} \right\| _ {\Sigma_ {t} ^ {- 1}} ^ {2} \leq \sigma^ {2} \log \left(\frac {\det (\Sigma_ {t}) \det (\Sigma_ {0}) ^ {- 1}}{\delta^ {2}}\right).\]

References

[1] Agarwal, A., Jiang, N., Kakade, S. M. & Sun, W. (2022). Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms. [2] Wikipedia. Markov’s inequality. [3] Wikipedia. Chernoff bound. [4] Wikipedia. Hoeffding’s inequality. [5] Harin Lee. Freedman’s Inequality.
entry.summary: A summary of key concentration inequalities used in the analysis of reinforcement learning algorithms.
